topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: From Spans to Bases

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Vectors as Arrows
sections.content: Briefly define a vector as a directed line segment with magnitude and direction. Introduce scalar multiplication and vector addition as the building blocks of the space.
sections.example: Visualizing a 2D plane: A vector v=(2,1) moves 2 steps East and 1 step North.

sections.title: Linear Combinations and Span
sections.content: Explain that a linear combination is a sum of vectors scaled by constants. The 'Span' is the set of all possible points reachable by combining these vectors. Use a graphical animation of a plane filling up.
sections.example: Two robots moving on a 2D floor: Robot A moves along vector u, Robot B along vector v. Their combined positions span the entire 2D floor.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundancy Rule
sections.content: Define linear dependence as a situation where one vector can be written as a combination of others. Visually, these vectors lie on the same line or plane. If they are 'dependent,' they don't add new directions to the span.
sections.example: Three characters walking in a line: If Person C is just walking along the path already covered by Person A and B, Person C is 'redundant'—the set is linearly dependent.

sections.title: Bases: The Minimalist Toolkit
sections.content: Introduce a 'Basis' as the most efficient set of vectors that span a space without redundancy. A basis must be linearly independent and span the entire space.
sections.example: The standard unit vectors (1,0) and (0,1) acting as the GPS grid of a map—they provide the simplest way to reach any location in the coordinate system.

sections.title: Summary and Synthesis
sections.content: Review: Span (Reach), Independence (Efficiency), and Basis (The perfect set). Connect these concepts to high-dimensional data processing.
sections.example: A 3D video game engine: Uses a basis of 3 vectors to define every object's position in 3D space.
